body:
Where the inquiry stands after three pieces: the objection and the rival were written independently against the account, and they land on the same distinction from different directions — the objection's memorial-versus-normative split is the rival's reconstruction-versus-divergence split restated. Two independent criticisms converging on one internal point is the strongest signal in the material, so I adopt it: 'we disagree about what the agreement meant' under changing schedules describes ambiguity exposed by circumstance, not, or not only, forgetting. The consequence is that a written record addresses at most one of the live readings, which neither critic claims to have ruled out.

What I use, and on what grounds. The rival's probe — ask each flatmate separately what they thought a past disputed agreement actually was, before building anything — is the piece I take up as the next move. My ground is specific: the objection showed that the account's proposed test (write it down, watch disputes fall) is non-discriminative, since either outcome can be read as supporting the memory reading, and the probe is the first instrument offered that discriminates before the household is restructured. It also folds the objection's re-ranked priority into itself: administering it requires talking to the avoiding friend about a concrete past event rather than about their avoidance, which is the rival's reframe and partly answers the account's own singling-out worry.

One sharpening. The rival proposed classifying the answers by scope, recurrence, or timing, but that only discriminates between the memory and ambiguity readings; the standing-negotiation reading has no signature there. Add a second axis: whether answers are task-referring ('the bins weren't part of it') or person-referring ('he never counts what I do'). Person-referring answers are what the standing reading predicts; task-referring answers are what the first two readings predict. This also touches a blind spot all three pieces share — nothing so far would surface felt load or fairness directly, and I don't think one flatmate can safely ask another a scorekeeping question. Person-referring vocabulary is how unfairness would become visible without being asked about.

What I revise. The sequencing. Each proposal on the table is the native remedy of one reading: the record belongs to the memory reading; the check-in belongs to the rival's ambiguity reading, since its real function is not memory but a scheduled renegotiation slot — the account's own phrase, stating the schedule change before it bites, describes re-contracting; and naming the pattern belongs to the avoidance-central and standing readings. None is reading-neutral, so none should go first. Probe first, then whichever instrument the answers point to, check-in last — its value flips most sharply across readings, being useful under the first two and, under the objection's reading, more of the conversation people are already leaving. This sides with the objection on order of operations, but on grounds the objection lacked: there is now an instrument to arbitrate the order rather than assert it.

What I reject. Two things. The prospective inference — 'record them now and drift will stop' — is supported by nothing shown; the objection's split between that and the retrospective possibility stands. And the account's framing of the note as 'just a visible record, not a moral ledger': the rival's point that 'A: dishes, Mon' is not self-interpreting, together with the account's own surveillance caveat, defeats the neutrality of the description. The tool may still be trialed; its innocence may not be assumed.

What stays open. Whether the avoidance predates the schedule changes; whether relocating the argument onto a record would be improvement or delay; and whether the probe is even administrable — the asker is a party, and if the disagreements concentrate on one person, the answers are compromised by the asking. I note without using it that infeasibility would itself be diagnostic: if nobody in the flat can ask one question without it becoming the argument, internal inquiry is exhausted and the mediator question the objection declined becomes salient.

For the person who asked: before any system, one short conversation with each flatmate, the same two questions — 'last time we agreed and later saw it differently, what did you think we had agreed?' and 'how are these conversations for you?' Say openly that you're asking everyone both questions. Don't adjudicate, don't relay answers between flatmates, don't propose fixes in the same conversation. Then choose the instrument based on the shape of what you heard. That is the whole current proposal; everything else is conditional on it.
commitments:
Claim-type uptake: I adopt the memorial-versus-normative distinction (the objection's and rival's shared point) as the working analytical tool, not as an established fact about this household. It is contestable, and I inherit the objection's own concession: if it turns out that in households like this the act of writing something down does shift what people take the agreement to be, the distinction loses practical bite and this revision of the account loses ground with it. That outcome would count as a revision of my position, not noise.

Criticism uptake: I take up the objection's rejection of the prospective inference and will not write as though any remedy follows from the diagnosis. My own rejection of the 'just a note' neutrality framing is a criticism whose grounds are internal to the exposed material; if a record were introduced and read by all three flatmates as innocuous, that would count against the rejection, and I'd accept it as overstated.

Application-type: the two-question probe is my main proposal, and its scope is narrow — one asker, two questions, no adjudication, no relaying. Its weakness is structural: the asker is a party to the disputes, recollection is already contested, and the probe measures current reports, not past agreements. It is informative about the shape of the disagreement space, not about what anyone originally said. My added classification axis (task-referring versus person-referring answers) is a proposed amendment, not a validated method; the categories need not be exhaustive, answers can be mixed, and I extend the rival's warning to my own axis — non-clustering answers must not be read as confirming whichever reading the asker already favors.

Pre-registered direction, stated so it can count against me: if the probe returns clean task-referring clustering around scope, recurrence, or timing, and a narrow practice of stating scope aloud at the moment of agreement then ends the recurring disputes, the avoidance-central and standing readings to which I gave weight lose relative standing, and my sequencing argument is weakened proportionally. Conversely, if answers are person-referring, I commit to deferring any record trial regardless of how tidy it would be, because under that result the record most plausibly relocates the argument rather than settling it — the rival's unanswered relocation question, kept open and made conditional.

Unresolved and not papered over: whether the probe is administrable by a participant at all; whether felt load and fairness can be surfaced directly rather than only through person-referring vocabulary, a gap my amendment does not close; and the mediator question, which I decline to rank exactly as the objection did, while naming the condition under which it becomes the salient next question — the probe's own infeasibility.

What I am not committing to: that any of the three readings is true of this flat, that anyone bears more work than anyone else, or that the household wants any intervention described here. What I actually propose to take up, if this continues: write the two questions and the answer-classification compactly enough that the flatmate could use them this week, and report what the household says rather than what fits a reading — inheriting the account's closing commitment to further inquiry, not to the truth of any account, including this one.
